![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14059897/assets/ac639fb08d54d2004aec96708ffd19bc080b028e739075687a84a09158cd4fd2.png)

Calculate ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path along a semicircle of radius $2,$ traversed from the point $(2,1)$ to the point $(-2,1),$ shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to $x$ along a path $C$ is equal to the net change in $x$ between the terminal and initial points:

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}x={x}_{2}-{x}_{1},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ is the $x$-coordinate of the terminal point, and ${x}_{1}$ is the $x$-coordinate of the initial point.

In our case, ${x}_{2}=-2$ and ${x}_{1}=2.$ Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}x={x}_{2}-{x}_{1}=(-2)-2=-4.
$$

- ${\int }_{-C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x=-{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x$

- ${\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{{C}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x-{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & =4-6 \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}

canonical_examples.problem:
Calculate $\displaystyle\int_C \,\textrm d x,$ where $C=C_1 \cup C_2$ is the path comprising of two line segments, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14059897/assets/3d408de0d50e2688aa0b35d8af39b6847cfdf21d5ec583320f0204384304fbc8.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to $x$ along a path $C$ is equal to the net change in $x$ between the terminal and initial points:

$$
\int_C \,\textrm d x = x_2 - x_1,
$$

where $x_2$ is the $x$-coordinate of the terminal point, and $x_1$ is the $x$-coordinate of the initial point.

In our case, $x_2 = -3$ and $x_1 = 3.$ Therefore,

$$
\int_C \,\textrm d x = x_2 - x_1 = (-3) - 3 = -6.
$$

canonical_examples.problem: If $\displaystyle\int_{C} f(x,y) \,\textrm d x= 8$ and $\displaystyle\int_{-C_1} f(x,y) \,\textrm d x= -2,$ calculate $\displaystyle\int_{-C_2} f(x,y) \,\textrm d x$ given that $C = C_1\cup C_2.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $C = C_1\cup C_2$ be a piecewise smooth path in the $xy$-plane, and let $-C$ be the curve consisting of the same points as $C$ but with the opposite orientation. 

For line integrals with respect to $x,$ we have the following properties:

- $\displaystyle\int_{-C} f(x,y)\,\textrm d x = -\int_{C} f(x,y)\,\textrm d x$

- $\displaystyle\int_{C} f(x,y)\,\textrm d x = \int_{C_1} f(x,y)\,\textrm d x + \int_{C_2} f(x,y)\,\textrm d x$

In our case, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\ 8 & =-{\int }_{-{C}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x-{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\ 8 & =-(-2)-{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\ 8 & =2-{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\ 6 & =-{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\int_{-C_2} f(x,y) \,\textrm d x = -6.
$$
